description: Invertebrate animals (sponges to insects to starfish), every kind of fish, the fish that crawled onto land, and the amphibians. Stops at the amniotes — reptiles, dinosaurs, birds and mammals live in other files.

nodes.name: Sponges
nodes.summary: The simplest animals alive: no brain, no muscles, no stomach — just a body full of holes and canals that pumps seawater through and strains out food.
facts: A sponge pushed through a fine sieve can reassemble itself from the separated cells.
One deep-sea glass sponge was estimated to be about 11,000 years old.
Chemical traces of sponges may be among the oldest signs of animal life in the rocks.

nodes.name: Comb jellies
nodes.summary: See-through sea creatures that swim by beating rows of tiny hairs called combs, which scatter light into shimmering rainbows. They look like jellyfish but are a completely separate, very ancient branch.
facts: They are the largest animals that swim using hair-like cilia.
A 2023 study of gene order suggests comb jellies, not sponges, were the very first branch off the animal family tree.
An accidentally introduced comb jelly devastated fisheries in the Black Sea in the 1980s.

nodes.name: Dickinsonia
nodes.summary: A flat, ribbed, oval creature of the Ediacaran seas, before the Cambrian explosion. For decades nobody knew if it was an animal, a lichen or a giant amoeba.
facts: In 2018 scientists found traces of cholesterol in Dickinsonia fossils — a molecule typical of animals.
Some grew to about 1.4 metres long yet were only millimetres thick, like a living bathmat.
It had no mouth or gut that we can see; it may have absorbed food from microbial mats beneath it.

nodes.name: Cnidarians
nodes.summary: Jellyfish, corals, sea anemones and hydras. They catch prey with stinging cells — microscopic harpoons — and have a single opening that serves as both mouth and bottom.
facts: Their stinging cells fire with an acceleration of over 5 million g — one of the fastest movements in nature.
Cnidarians have no brain, just a loose net of nerves.

nodes.name: Corals & sea anemones
nodes.summary: Cnidarians that never become swimming jellyfish. They spend their whole lives as flower-like polyps stuck to the sea floor.

nodes.name: Sea anemones
nodes.summary: Squishy, flower-shaped predators that wave stinging tentacles to catch small fish and shrimp. Clownfish famously live safely among them.
facts: Most anemones barely move, but some can glide slowly on their base or even swim away from danger.
The tiny starlet sea anemone has nearly as many genes as a human.

nodes.name: Stony corals
nodes.summary: Tiny polyps that build limestone skeletons and, together with algae living inside them, construct coral reefs — home to about a quarter of all ocean species.
facts: The Great Barrier Reef is about 2,300 km long — the largest structure built by living things, visible from space.
Corals get their colours from algae living in their cells; when stressed by hot water they expel them and turn white (bleaching).

nodes.name: Medusozoans
nodes.summary: The cnidarians that can turn into a free-swimming, bell-shaped medusa — a jellyfish. Includes true jellyfish, box jellyfish and hydras.

nodes.name: True jellyfish
nodes.summary: Pulsing bells of jelly trailing stinging tentacles. Jellyfish have drifted through the oceans for over 500 million years — longer than dinosaurs, trees or fish have existed.
facts: Jellyfish are about 95% water and have no brain, heart or bones.
One washed-up lion's mane jellyfish had tentacles about 37 metres long — longer than a blue whale.

nodes.name: Box jellyfish
nodes.summary: Cube-shaped jellyfish that actively hunt instead of drifting. Some, like the Australian sea wasp, carry some of the most dangerous venom in the animal world.
facts: Box jellyfish have 24 eyes, and some of them have lenses like ours.
They can steer around obstacles — impressive for an animal with no brain.

nodes.name: Hydra
nodes.summary: A tiny freshwater polyp, about a centimetre long, related to jellyfish. Cut it into pieces and each piece can grow into a whole new hydra.
facts: It is named after the many-headed monster of Greek myth that regrew its heads.
Studies of hydras kept for years found no sign that they age at all.

nodes.name: Immortal jellyfish
nodes.summary: A jellyfish smaller than your little fingernail that can cheat death: when injured or starving, the adult turns back into a baby polyp and starts life again.
facts: In theory it can repeat this cycle again and again — but in practice most are eaten or die of disease.
It is a hydrozoan, a cousin of Hydra, not a true jellyfish.

nodes.name: Kimberella
nodes.summary: A slug-like Ediacaran animal that crawled over microbial mats and scraped them for food. It may be one of the earliest relatives of molluscs.
facts: Fan-shaped scratch marks left by its feeding are found right next to its fossils.
Its fossils come from Australia and the White Sea coast of Russia.

nodes.name: Lophotrochozoans
nodes.summary: A huge branch of soft-bodied animals that grow without moulting: flatworms, segmented worms, snails, clams and octopuses.

nodes.name: Flatworms
nodes.summary: Paper-thin worms with no lungs or blood vessels and a gut with just one opening. They include free-living planarians and parasitic tapeworms and flukes.
facts: A planarian can regrow a whole body from a fragment as small as 1/279th of the original.
Some tapeworms living in human guts can grow longer than 10 metres.

nodes.name: Segmented worms
nodes.summary: Worms built from a chain of repeated ring-like segments: earthworms, leeches and thousands of colourful bristle worms in the sea.

nodes.name: Earthworms
nodes.summary: Underground ploughs that eat soil, digest the rotting bits and leave behind rich, airy earth that plants love.
facts: Charles Darwin's last book, in 1881, was all about earthworms.
Earthworms breathe through their skin, which is why they come up when rain floods their burrows.
Australia's giant Gippsland earthworm can reach about 3 metres long.

nodes.name: Leeches
nodes.summary: Segmented worms with a sucker at each end. Some drink blood, injecting chemicals that numb the bite and stop blood from clotting.
facts: Doctors still use medicinal leeches to rescue reattached fingers and ears; US regulators approved them as a medical device in 2004.
The medicinal leech has ten eyes.

nodes.name: Molluscs
nodes.summary: Soft-bodied animals, often protected by a shell: snails, clams and the brainy octopuses and squid. With around 85,000 living species they are the second-biggest animal phylum.
facts: Most molluscs feed with a radula — a tongue covered in rows of tiny teeth.
Chitons have teeth capped with magnetite, a magnetic iron mineral.

nodes.name: Snails & slugs
nodes.summary: Molluscs that crawl on a single muscular foot. The only molluscs to conquer dry land, they range from garden snails to venomous cone snails and dazzling sea slugs.
facts: A garden snail's tongue carries thousands of microscopic teeth.
Slugs are snails that lost their shells — and that happened several separate times.
Cone snail venom is so potent it has been turned into a powerful painkiller.

nodes.name: Clams, oysters & mussels
nodes.summary: Molluscs living inside two hinged shells. They have no head at all and filter food from the water — some, like oysters, make pearls.
facts: An ocean quahog clam nicknamed Ming was 507 years old — the oldest individual animal ever aged precisely.
A scallop can have up to 200 eyes along the edge of its shell.

nodes.name: Cephalopods
nodes.summary: The 'head-foot' molluscs: octopuses, squid, cuttlefish and nautiluses. Fast, clever, jet-propelled hunters with arms growing straight out of their heads.
facts: They have blue blood and three hearts.
Many can change colour in a fraction of a second — even though most are colour-blind.

nodes.name: Nautiluses
nodes.summary: The last cephalopods with an outer shell, divided into gas-filled chambers that work like a submarine's ballast tanks. Their lineage has barely changed for hundreds of millions of years.
facts: Nautiloids have survived all five of Earth's great mass extinctions.
A nautilus has up to 90 tentacles — with no suckers.

nodes.name: Ammonites
nodes.summary: Squid-like animals in coiled, chambered shells that filled the seas for over 340 million years. They vanished with the dinosaurs, leaving countless spiral fossils.
facts: The biggest ammonite shells were nearly 2 metres across.
They are named after the Egyptian god Ammon, who was shown with curled ram's horns.
Geologists use ammonite species to date rocks precisely.

nodes.name: Octopuses, squid & cuttlefish
nodes.summary: Cephalopods that moved their shell inside their body or lost it altogether, trading armour for speed, camouflage and big brains.

nodes.name: Belemnites
nodes.summary: Squid-like hunters of the dinosaur-age seas. Their bullet-shaped internal shells are such common fossils that people once thought they were thunderbolts.
facts: In 2009 scientists drew a picture using ink from a 150-million-year-old fossil belemnite ink sac.
Belemnite arm hooks are often found in the fossil stomachs of ichthyosaurs, which loved to eat them.

nodes.name: Octopuses
nodes.summary: Eight-armed escape artists and puzzle solvers, often called the most intelligent invertebrates. They change colour and texture to vanish against rocks.
facts: About two-thirds of an octopus's neurons are in its arms, which can taste what they touch.
An octopus can squeeze through any hole bigger than its hard beak.
Veined octopuses carry coconut shells around to use as portable shelters.

nodes.name: Squid
nodes.summary: Streamlined, ten-armed cephalopods that shoot through the water by jet propulsion. Some even launch themselves into the air and glide.
facts: Squid have giant nerve fibres so thick that studying them helped scientists win a Nobel Prize for explaining how nerves work.
Japanese flying squid have been seen gliding about 30 metres above the waves.

nodes.name: Giant squid
nodes.summary: A deep-sea giant up to about 12 metres long and the likely source of sea-monster legends like the kraken. It battles sperm whales in the dark.
facts: Its eyes can be about 27 cm across — as big as a dinner plate.
Nobody photographed a live giant squid in the wild until 2004, and it was first filmed in 2012.
Sperm whales often carry round scars from giant squid suckers.

nodes.name: Moulting animals
nodes.summary: Animals that grow by shedding their outer skin or shell: roundworms, water bears, velvet worms and all arthropods. Together they make up most of the animals on Earth.

nodes.name: Roundworms
nodes.summary: Tiny, smooth, thread-like worms living almost everywhere: in soil, oceans, hot springs, ice — and inside plants and animals. Most are harmless; some cause disease.
facts: A 2019 study estimated there are about 57 billion soil nematodes for every person on Earth.
One species was found living 1.3 km underground in a South African gold mine.

nodes.name: C. elegans
nodes.summary: A see-through, millimetre-long soil worm that became one of biology's superstars. Scientists know the fate of every single one of its cells.
facts: An adult (hermaphrodite) has exactly 959 body cells, 302 of them neurons.
It was the first animal to have its whole genome sequenced, in 1998.
C. elegans worms survived the Space Shuttle Columbia disaster in 2003.

nodes.name: Tardigrades
nodes.summary: Chubby, eight-legged 'water bears' about half a millimetre long. By drying up into a shrivelled 'tun' they survive freezing, boiling, radiation and even outer space.
facts: In 2007 tardigrades survived 10 days exposed to the vacuum of space.
A capsule of dried tardigrades crash-landed on the Moon with the Israeli Beresheet probe in 2019.

nodes.name: Velvet worms
nodes.summary: Soft, velvety, many-legged forest hunters, close cousins of the arthropods. They trap insects by squirting jets of sticky slime.
facts: Their stubby legs have no joints — they are stiffened by fluid pressure, like water balloons.
Their ancestors lived in Cambrian seas; today they live only on land.

nodes.name: Hallucigenia
nodes.summary: A Cambrian 'lobopodian' worm with spiny legs and two rows of spines on its back — an early relative of velvet worms. Its name means 'dream-like'.
facts: It was first reconstructed upside down, walking on its spines.
Scientists also mixed up its head and tail; its tiny head and teeth were only identified in 2015.

nodes.name: Arthropods
nodes.summary: Animals with jointed legs and an armoured exoskeleton: insects, spiders, crabs, centipedes and extinct trilobites. The most successful body plan in animal history.
facts: More than three-quarters of all known animal species are arthropods.
Their exoskeleton is made of chitin — the same material as fungal cell walls.

nodes.name: Anomalocaris
nodes.summary: A Cambrian top predator with two spiny grasping arms, a ring-shaped mouth and big compound eyes. At about half a metre long it was a giant when most animals were smaller than your finger.
facts: Its fossil pieces were first described as three different animals: a shrimp, a jellyfish and a sea cucumber.
Its name means 'abnormal shrimp'.
Fossil eyes of a close radiodont relative from Australia had more than 16,000 lenses each.

nodes.name: Opabinia
nodes.summary: A finger-sized Cambrian oddball with five eyes and a long, flexible nozzle tipped with a claw for grabbing food. An early relative of arthropods from the Burgess Shale.
facts: When its reconstruction was first shown at a scientific meeting in 1972, the audience burst out laughing.

nodes.name: Trilobites
nodes.summary: Armoured sea arthropods that crawled ancient sea floors for almost 270 million years. Many could roll up into a ball like a woodlouse.
facts: Their eyes had lenses made of the mineral calcite — essentially stone eyes.
Over 20,000 species are known.
The last trilobites died in the Great Dying, 252 million years ago.

nodes.name: Chelicerates
nodes.summary: Arthropods with no antennae and pincer- or fang-like mouthparts called chelicerae: spiders, scorpions, ticks, horseshoe crabs and the extinct sea scorpions.

nodes.name: Sea scorpions
nodes.summary: Scorpion-like predators of ancient seas, lagoons and rivers. Some, like Jaekelopterus, grew to around 2.5 metres — the largest arthropods that ever lived.
facts: Jaekelopterus had a claw about 36 cm long.
Despite the name they were not true scorpions, and many lived in fresh water.

nodes.name: Horseshoe crabs
nodes.summary: Not crabs at all but armoured cousins of spiders, from a lineage whose oldest fossils are about 445 million years old. Every spring they crowd onto beaches to lay eggs.
facts: Their blue blood is used to test vaccines and medicines for dangerous bacterial toxins.
They have ten eyes, including some on their tail.

nodes.name: Arachnids
nodes.summary: Eight-legged chelicerates — spiders, scorpions, ticks, mites and harvestmen. Most can't chew, so they liquefy their prey and slurp it up.

nodes.name: Spiders
nodes.summary: Silk-spinning, eight-legged predators found on every continent except Antarctica. About 50,000 species weave webs, jump, lurk in burrows or even hunt underwater.
facts: The silk of Darwin's bark spider is tougher than Kevlar.
Almost all spiders are venomous, but only a few dozen species are dangerous to people.
Male peacock spiders win mates with colourful dance routines.

nodes.name: Scorpions
nodes.summary: Arachnids with grasping pincers and a venomous sting curled over their back. Their ancestors lived in water, and scorpions were among the early animals to colonise land.
facts: Scorpions glow blue-green under ultraviolet light.
Some can survive a whole year without eating.

nodes.name: Ticks
nodes.summary: Blood-drinking relatives of mites that wait on grass tips for an animal to brush past. They can spread diseases such as Lyme disease.
facts: A feeding female tick can swell to about 100 times her starting weight.
A tick was found in 99-million-year-old amber still clinging to a dinosaur feather.

nodes.name: Myriapods
nodes.summary: Many-legged arthropods with long, segmented bodies: centipedes and millipedes. They were among the very first animals to leave the water.

nodes.name: Centipedes
nodes.summary: Fast, venomous hunters with one pair of legs per body segment. Their front legs have turned into poison fangs.
facts: Centipedes always have an odd number of leg pairs, so none has exactly 100 legs.
The Amazonian giant centipede can catch bats in mid-air from cave ceilings.

nodes.name: Millipedes
nodes.summary: Slow, peaceful recyclers of dead leaves with two pairs of legs on most segments. Many defend themselves by oozing smelly or toxic chemicals.
facts: In 2021 a millipede with 1,306 legs was discovered deep underground in Australia — the first to truly have over a thousand.
A Scottish fossil millipede over 410 million years old is one of the oldest known land animals.

nodes.name: Arthropleura
nodes.summary: A giant millipede relative up to about 2.6 metres long that roamed the Carboniferous coal forests — the biggest land invertebrate of all time.
facts: Its fossil trackways can be around half a metre wide.
Fossil heads described in 2024 confirmed it was a millipede, not a centipede.

nodes.name: Crustaceans & insects
nodes.summary: Genes reveal a surprise: insects evolved from within the crustaceans. In a sense, a bee is a land-going shrimp.

nodes.name: Malacostracans
nodes.summary: The biggest group of crustaceans: crabs, lobsters, shrimp, krill and woodlice — about 40,000 species in all.

nodes.name: Crabs
nodes.summary: Crustaceans with a short tail tucked under a broad shell, famous for walking sideways. They live in oceans, rivers and even up trees.
facts: The crab body shape evolved independently at least five times — biologists call it 'carcinisation'.
The Japanese spider crab's legs can span about 3.7 metres.

nodes.name: Lobsters
nodes.summary: Big-clawed crustaceans that hide in rocky crevices by day. They keep growing and moulting throughout their long lives.
facts: Lobsters taste with their legs and grind food with teeth inside their stomach.
Lobster blood is colourless until it meets air, when it turns blue.

nodes.name: Shrimp
nodes.summary: Small swimming crustaceans with long antennae and fanned tails, found from coral reefs to deep-sea vents.
facts: A pistol shrimp snaps its claw so fast it creates a bubble that briefly gets nearly as hot as the surface of the Sun.
Cleaner shrimp run 'stations' where fish queue up to have parasites picked off.

nodes.name: Krill
nodes.summary: Finger-length, shrimp-like swarmers that feed whales, penguins, seals and fish. Antarctic krill may be the most abundant wild animal on Earth by weight.
facts: The total weight of Antarctic krill is estimated at hundreds of millions of tonnes.
A blue whale can eat around 16 tonnes of krill in a single day.
Krill glow with their own blue-green light.

nodes.name: Woodlice
nodes.summary: Crustaceans that moved onto land and now live under logs and stones. Pill bugs can roll into a perfect armoured ball.
facts: They breathe with lung-like organs on the underside of their tail end, which must stay damp.
Instead of peeing, woodlice get rid of waste as ammonia gas through their shell.

nodes.name: Barnacles
nodes.summary: Crustaceans that glue their heads to rocks, ships and whales, build a shell house, and kick food into their mouths with feathery legs.
facts: Charles Darwin spent eight years studying barnacles.
Relative to body size, barnacles have the longest penis of any animal — up to eight times their body length.

nodes.name: Insects
nodes.summary: Six legs, three body parts and, usually, wings. With over a million named species, insects are the most diverse animals ever — and the first to fly.
facts: Insects were flying about 100 million years before the first pterosaurs.
At any moment there may be around 10 quintillion (10,000,000,000,000,000,000) insects alive.

nodes.name: Silverfish
nodes.summary: Shiny, wingless, wriggling insects from an ancient lineage that split off before insects learned to fly. They nibble the starch in book glue and wallpaper paste.
facts: Unlike most insects, silverfish keep moulting all their adult lives.
They can live up to eight years and survive months without food.

nodes.name: Dragonflies & damselflies
nodes.summary: Aerial hunters that can hover, fly backwards and snatch prey in mid-air. Their ancestors were some of the first flying animals.
facts: In lab tests dragonflies caught about 95% of the prey they chased.
Their young live underwater and move by squirting water out of their bottoms.

nodes.name: Meganeura
nodes.summary: A Carboniferous 'griffinfly' — a cousin of dragonflies — with a wingspan of about 70 cm, as wide as a hawk's. One of the largest flying insects ever.
facts: Oxygen levels in the Carboniferous air were higher than today, which may have helped insects grow so large.
Its fossils were found in coal mines at Commentry, France.

nodes.name: Cockroaches
nodes.summary: Tough, flat, fast-running insects with roots in the coal-swamp forests. Of about 4,600 species, only around 30 bother people.
facts: A cockroach can live for about a week without its head.
Roach-like insects were scuttling around before the first dinosaurs.

nodes.name: Termites
nodes.summary: Social insects that live in huge colonies ruled by a king and queen. DNA shows they are really a branch of the cockroach family that went social.
facts: African termite mounds have such good natural ventilation that architects have copied them for buildings.
A termite queen can lay thousands of eggs a day.

nodes.name: Grasshoppers & locusts
nodes.summary: Plant-munching jumpers with powerful back legs. Locusts are grasshoppers that, when crowded, change colour and behaviour and form enormous swarms.
facts: Grasshoppers hear with ears on the sides of their belly.
An 1875 swarm of Rocky Mountain locusts was estimated at over 10 trillion insects — yet the species was extinct by about 1902.

nodes.name: Insects with complete metamorphosis
nodes.summary: Insects whose young are grubs, maggots or caterpillars that rebuild themselves inside a pupa. This trick lets babies and adults live completely different lives — and it made them wildly successful.
facts: Most insect species alive today belong to this group.

nodes.name: Beetles
nodes.summary: Insects whose front wings became hard armoured covers. With about 400,000 described species, roughly one in four known animals is a beetle.
facts: Bombardier beetles fire a boiling-hot chemical spray from their rear end.
Dung beetles can steer by the glow of the Milky Way.

nodes.name: Butterflies & moths
nodes.summary: Insects with wings covered in tiny coloured scales and caterpillars for babies. Butterflies are really a colourful, day-flying branch of the moths.
facts: Fossil wing scales show moths existed before flowers did.
There are about ten times as many moth species as butterfly species.

nodes.name: Silkworm
nodes.summary: The caterpillar of a fully domesticated moth. Each spins a cocoon from a single silk thread, and its silk built the Silk Road.
facts: Adult silkworm moths cannot fly, and the species no longer exists in the wild.
One cocoon is made of a single thread that can be over a kilometre long.
nodes.origin: Domesticated in China around 5,000 years ago from the wild silk moth Bombyx mandarina. For centuries China guarded the secret of silk-making.

nodes.name: Wasps, bees & ants
nodes.summary: Insects with two pairs of linked wings and, often, a narrow 'wasp waist'. Bees and ants are both specialised kinds of wasp.
facts: Males usually hatch from unfertilised eggs — so they have a mother but no father.

nodes.name: Ants
nodes.summary: Social insects that live in colonies of up to millions, divide their labour, wage wars and farm. They descend from wasps.
facts: A 2022 study estimated there are about 20 quadrillion ants on Earth.
All the ants together outweigh all wild birds and wild mammals combined.
Leafcutter ants were farming fungus millions of years before humans farmed anything.

nodes.name: Bees
nodes.summary: Wasps that went vegetarian, feeding their young on pollen and nectar instead of prey. They became the most important pollinators of flowers and crops.
facts: There are about 20,000 bee species, and most live alone, not in hives.
Bees can see ultraviolet patterns on flowers that are invisible to us.

nodes.name: Honeybee
nodes.summary: A social bee living in colonies of tens of thousands, kept by people for honey and wax and to pollinate crops. Workers tell each other where flowers are by dancing.
facts: Karl von Frisch won a Nobel Prize in 1973 for decoding the honeybee 'waggle dance'.
A worker bee makes only about a twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in its whole life.
nodes.origin: Only semi-domesticated: people collected wild honey for tens of thousands of years, beeswax traces in Anatolian pottery date back about 9,000 years, and Egyptians kept bees in hives by around 4,500 years ago. Kept colonies can still swarm and go wild.

nodes.name: Social wasps
nodes.summary: Yellowjackets, hornets and paper wasps. They build nests from wood they chew into paper and help gardens by hunting caterpillars and flies.
facts: Paper wasps can recognise each other's faces.
In 1719 a French scientist watching wasps suggested humans could make paper from wood too.

nodes.name: True flies
nodes.summary: Insects with just one pair of wings; the back pair shrank into tiny knobs that work like gyroscopes. Includes houseflies, mosquitoes and fruit flies.
facts: Houseflies taste food with their feet.
Flies are among the most important pollinators after bees.

nodes.name: Mosquitoes
nodes.summary: Small flies whose females drink blood to make their eggs. By spreading malaria and other diseases they are the deadliest animals to humans.
facts: Only female mosquitoes bite; males drink nectar.
They find you partly by sensing the carbon dioxide you breathe out.

nodes.name: Fruit fly
nodes.summary: A tiny fly that hangs around ripe fruit and has been a laboratory superstar for over a century, revealing how genes work.
facts: Fruit flies were the first animals deliberately sent into space, on a rocket in 1947.
About three-quarters of human disease genes have a recognisable match in the fruit fly.
Fruit-fly research has led to several Nobel Prizes.

nodes.name: Echinoderms
nodes.summary: Spiny-skinned sea animals built in fives: starfish, sea urchins, sea cucumbers and feather stars. They walk on hundreds of water-powered tube feet.
facts: Their larvae are left-right symmetrical like us; the five-part body only appears as they grow up.
They have no brain.

nodes.name: Starfish
nodes.summary: Sea stars that creep over rocks hunting clams and snails. Not fish at all, they eat by pushing their stomach out of their body and digesting prey on the spot.
facts: Many can regrow lost arms, and some can regrow a whole body from one arm.
There is a simple eye at the tip of each arm.

nodes.name: Sea urchins
nodes.summary: Spiny balls that graze algae with a five-toothed jaw. Too many of them, and they can mow down entire kelp forests.
facts: Their jaw is called 'Aristotle's lantern' and its teeth sharpen themselves.
Red sea urchins can live for over 200 years.

nodes.name: Sea cucumbers
nodes.summary: Soft, sausage-shaped echinoderms that vacuum the sea floor. When threatened, some shoot out sticky threads or even their own guts — and grow new ones.
facts: Many breathe through their bottoms.
Small pearlfish live inside sea cucumbers, entering through the anus.

nodes.name: Acorn worms
nodes.summary: Burrowing sea worms with gill slits in their throat — the same feature that fish have. They are close cousins of echinoderms and distant cousins of us.
facts: The extinct graptolites, common fossils in old rocks, were colonial hemichordates.

nodes.name: Lancelets
nodes.summary: Small, eel-like filter feeders that bury themselves in sand. With a notochord, nerve cord and muscle blocks but no skull, bones or jaws, they look like a blueprint for a fish.
facts: Lancelets have no true heart — their blood is pushed along by contracting vessels.
They are eaten as a local delicacy around Xiamen in China.

nodes.name: Tunicates
nodes.summary: Sea squirts and their relatives — our closest living invertebrate relatives. Their larvae look like tiny tadpoles, but adults glue themselves down and become filter-feeding bags.
facts: When a sea squirt settles down, it absorbs most of its own tail, notochord and larval nervous system.
Tunicates are the only animals that can make cellulose, the stuff of plant cell walls.

nodes.name: Pikaia
nodes.summary: A 5-cm, ribbon-shaped swimmer from the Burgess Shale with a notochord and zig-zag muscle blocks — one of the earliest known chordates.
facts: It was once celebrated as the ancestor of all vertebrates; it is now seen as a primitive cousin.

nodes.name: Haikouichthys
nodes.summary: A 2.5-cm swimmer from 518-million-year-old rocks in China, with eyes, gill pouches and fin folds. It is one of the earliest known vertebrates — a fish before fish had jaws.
facts: Its fossils come from the Chengjiang site in Yunnan, famous for preserving soft bodies.

nodes.name: Jawless fish
nodes.summary: The last survivors of the jawless fish that once ruled the seas: lampreys and hagfish, with round mouths and no paired fins.

nodes.name: Lampreys
nodes.summary: Eel-like jawless fish with a round sucker mouth full of rasping teeth. Many latch onto other fish and drink their blood.
facts: Sea lampreys invaded North America's Great Lakes through shipping canals and devastated fisheries.
A medieval chronicler wrote that King Henry I of England died from eating 'a surfeit of lampreys' in 1135.

nodes.name: Hagfish
nodes.summary: Slimy, eel-shaped scavengers of the deep sea floor that burrow into dead whales. They have a skull but barely any backbone.
facts: A hagfish can turn a bucket of seawater into gooey slime in moments.
To clean off slime or tear food, hagfish tie their bodies in a knot.

nodes.name: Conodonts
nodes.summary: Eel-like early vertebrates known mostly from their tiny tooth-like fossils, which are found by the billion in ancient rocks.
facts: Their teeth were discovered in 1856, but nobody knew what animal they came from until a body fossil turned up in Scotland in 1983.
Geologists use the colour of conodont teeth to tell how hot rocks once got — useful for finding oil.

nodes.name: Armoured jawless fish
nodes.summary: Jawless fish covered in bony armour plates, which sucked or scooped food from the sea floor. They were cousins of the ancestors of jawed fish.
facts: Their armour is among the earliest bone ever to evolve, including dentine — the same tissue in your teeth.

nodes.name: Placoderms
nodes.summary: Armour-plated fish with some of the first jaws, which ruled Devonian seas and rivers before vanishing at the end of that period.
facts: A 380-million-year-old placoderm fossil, Materpiscis, contains an embryo with an umbilical cord — the oldest known live birth.

nodes.name: Dunkleosteus
nodes.summary: A huge armour-headed placoderm and one of the first vertebrate superpredators. Instead of teeth it had self-sharpening bony blades that could slice through armour.
facts: It had one of the most powerful bites of any fish, and could open its jaws in a fiftieth of a second.
A 2023 study estimated it at about 4 metres long — smaller than older guesses, but much bulkier.

nodes.name: Spiny sharks
nodes.summary: Small, early jawed fish with sharp spines in front of almost every fin. They were probably early relatives of the sharks.
facts: They are some of the oldest jawed fish known, from fossil scales over 430 million years old.

nodes.name: Cartilaginous fish
nodes.summary: Sharks, rays and chimaeras, whose skeletons are made of flexible cartilage instead of bone and whose skin is covered in tiny tooth-like scales.
facts: They can sense the faint electric fields made by other animals' heartbeats.

nodes.name: Chimaeras
nodes.summary: Eerie deep-sea 'ghost sharks' with big eyes and rabbit-like tooth plates, from a lineage that split from sharks over 400 million years ago.
facts: Males carry a toothed, retractable clasper on their forehead used for mating.
The elephant shark, a chimaera, has the slowest-evolving genome of any known vertebrate.

nodes.name: Sharks & rays
nodes.summary: The shark-and-ray branch of cartilaginous fish. Their lineage is older than trees and has survived four of the big five mass extinctions.

nodes.name: Sharks
nodes.summary: Streamlined hunters with rows of replaceable teeth and superb senses. Shark-like fish swam over 400 million years ago; modern sharks split from rays around 290 million years ago.
facts: Some sharks lose and replace tens of thousands of teeth in a lifetime.
The Greenland shark may live for around 400 years — the longest-lived vertebrate known.

nodes.name: Great white shark
nodes.summary: The world's largest predatory fish, up to about 6 metres long, hunting seals and sea lions with surprise attacks from below.
facts: Great whites can leap completely out of the water when ambushing seals.
They keep their muscles, eyes and brain warmer than the surrounding sea.

nodes.name: Megalodon
nodes.summary: The biggest predatory shark that ever lived, probably 15 metres or more long, which hunted whales. It is known mostly from huge fossil teeth.
facts: Its teeth could be 18 cm long — bigger than a human hand.
It was not the ancestor of the great white but a distant cousin; competition with great whites may have helped drive it extinct.

nodes.name: Whale shark
nodes.summary: The largest fish alive, longer than a bus, yet it eats only plankton and small fish sifted from the water. Gentle enough for divers to swim alongside.
facts: Each whale shark's spot pattern is unique, and scientists identify them using software designed for mapping stars.
Whale sharks have tiny teeth covering their eyeballs.

nodes.name: Hammerhead sharks
nodes.summary: Sharks with a wide, flattened head shaped like a hammer, packed with sensors for finding prey hidden in sand.
facts: The hammer-shaped head gives them excellent depth perception and a wide field of view.
The bonnethead, a small hammerhead, eats and digests seagrass — the first known omnivorous shark.

nodes.name: Rays & skates
nodes.summary: Flattened relatives of sharks that 'fly' through the water on wing-like fins: stingrays, electric rays, sawfish and giant mantas.
facts: Electric rays can deliver shocks of over 200 volts; ancient Romans used them to treat headaches.
Manta rays have one of the largest brain-to-body ratios of any fish.

nodes.name: Ray-finned fish
nodes.summary: Fish whose fins are thin webs of skin held up by bony spines. With over 30,000 species, they make up about half of all vertebrates alive.
facts: They live everywhere from mountain streams at 5,000 m to ocean trenches 8,000 m deep.

nodes.name: Sturgeons
nodes.summary: Huge, armour-plated river fish from an ancient branch of ray-finned fish, little changed since the age of dinosaurs. Their eggs are sold as caviar.
facts: Beluga sturgeons can grow longer than a car and live for over 100 years.
Sturgeons are the most threatened group of animals assessed by the IUCN.

nodes.name: Gars
nodes.summary: Long-snouted, needle-toothed North American fish covered in tough, diamond-shaped scales. They can gulp air when water runs low on oxygen.
facts: Their scales are so hard that Native Americans used them as arrowheads.
Gar eggs are poisonous to people.

nodes.name: Teleosts
nodes.summary: The 'perfect bones' fish — about 96% of all fish species, from goldfish to tuna. Their jaws can shoot forward to snatch food.
facts: Their ancestor copied its whole genome by accident, giving teleosts spare genes to evolve new tricks.

nodes.name: Eels
nodes.summary: Snake-shaped fish of rivers, reefs and the deep sea. Their babies are see-through, leaf-shaped larvae that drift across oceans.
facts: European eels swim thousands of kilometres to the Sargasso Sea to breed — yet nobody has ever seen them spawn in the wild.
Aristotle thought eels grew out of mud.
The electric eel isn't a true eel — it's a knifefish.

nodes.name: Piranhas
nodes.summary: South American river fish with razor-sharp, interlocking teeth. Their man-eating reputation is mostly exaggerated: many eat fruit, seeds, scales and scraps.
facts: Red-bellied piranhas make barking sounds.
They replace their teeth one whole side of the jaw at a time.

nodes.name: Carps & minnows
nodes.summary: The largest order of freshwater fish, with over 4,000 species, including carp, minnows, goldfish and zebrafish.
facts: They have no teeth in their mouths — they chew with teeth in their throat.

nodes.name: Zebrafish
nodes.summary: A small striped minnow from South Asia that became a key lab animal: its see-through embryos let scientists watch organs form in real time.
facts: Zebrafish can regrow damaged heart muscle, fins, and even parts of the spinal cord.

nodes.name: Goldfish
nodes.summary: One of the first fish ever domesticated, bred in China from dull grey-green wild carp into dozens of fancy forms with bubble eyes and flowing tails.
facts: Goldfish can remember things for months — the '3-second memory' is a myth.
Goldfish released into lakes can grow as big as a football and become invasive pests.
nodes.origin: Domesticated in China from wild crucian-type carp (Prussian / silver crucian carp, genus Carassius). Gold-coloured mutants were kept in Buddhist 'mercy ponds' over 1,000 years ago, and by the Song dynasty (960–1279) people were breeding them for colour; goldfish reached Japan around 1500 and Europe in the 1600s.

nodes.name: Koi
nodes.summary: Colourful ornamental carp bred in Japan from the Amur carp, prized in garden ponds for their red, white, black and gold patterns.
facts: Their Japanese name, nishikigoi, means 'brocaded carp'.
A champion koi sold for about 1.8 million US dollars in 2018.
nodes.origin: Carp were farmed for food in China for over 2,000 years. Rice farmers around Niigata, Japan, began breeding colourful mutants of the Amur carp in the early 1800s, creating modern koi.

nodes.name: Salmon & trout
nodes.summary: Powerful fish that hatch in rivers, grow up at sea, then fight their way upstream — leaping waterfalls — to spawn where they were born.
facts: Salmon find their home stream partly by its unique smell.
Bears dragging salmon into forests fertilise the trees with ocean nutrients.
Salmon flesh is pink because of pigments from the krill and shrimp they eat.

nodes.name: Cod
nodes.summary: Cold-water fish that fed Europe and North America for centuries and powered fishing empires — until overfishing crashed their numbers.
facts: The Grand Banks cod fishery off Canada collapsed in 1992, putting tens of thousands of people out of work.
Atlantic cod lack a whole branch of the immune system that most vertebrates rely on.
A big female cod can release millions of eggs in a season.

nodes.name: Perch-like fish
nodes.summary: The great explosion of spiny-finned fish after the age of dinosaurs: tuna, seahorses, clownfish, anglerfish, pufferfish and flatfish. Nearly a quarter of all vertebrate species.

nodes.name: Tuna
nodes.summary: Torpedo-shaped ocean racers that never stop swimming, crossing whole oceans on their migrations.
facts: Tuna keep their bodies warmer than the water, like built-in engines.
They must keep swimming to push water over their gills.
A single bluefin tuna sold for about 3.1 million US dollars in Tokyo in 2019.

nodes.name: Seahorses
nodes.summary: Upright-swimming fish with a horse-like head and a grasping tail. In seahorses it is the father that gets pregnant and gives birth.
facts: The dwarf seahorse is the slowest fish known, moving about 1.5 metres per hour.
Seahorses have no stomach and must eat almost constantly.

nodes.name: Clownfish
nodes.summary: Orange-and-white reef fish that live safely inside stinging sea anemones, protected by a special coat of mucus.
facts: All clownfish hatch male; if a group's female dies, the biggest male turns into a female.
In return for shelter, clownfish clean their anemone and chase off fish that would eat it.

nodes.name: Anglerfish
nodes.summary: Fish that fish: a fin spine on their head works as a fishing rod with a lure. In the deep sea the lure glows with light made by bacteria.
facts: In some deep-sea anglerfish, the tiny male bites the female and permanently fuses to her body.
Scientists found these anglerfish have switched off parts of their immune system so the fusion isn't rejected.

nodes.name: Coelacanths
nodes.summary: Lobe-finned 'living fossils' thought to have died out with the dinosaurs — until a living one turned up in a South African fisherman's catch in 1938.
facts: Museum curator Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer spotted the 1938 coelacanth among the catch and saved it.
A second species was found in an Indonesian fish market in 1997.
Coelacanths can live about 100 years and are pregnant for about five years.

nodes.name: Lungfish
nodes.summary: Air-breathing fish with real lungs — the closest living fish relatives of four-legged animals, including us. Some survive droughts sealed in mud cocoons.
facts: The South American lungfish has about 30 times more DNA than a human — the largest animal genome ever sequenced.
An Australian lungfish called Granddad lived at a Chicago aquarium from 1933 until 2017.

nodes.name: Eusthenopteron
nodes.summary: A Devonian lobe-finned fish whose fins hide the same bones as your arm: one upper bone, then two lower bones.
facts: Thousands of its fossils come from Miguasha in Quebec, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
It is one of the most thoroughly studied fossil fish in the world.

nodes.name: Panderichthys
nodes.summary: A flat-headed, crocodile-like fish with eyes on top of its head, prowling shallow Devonian waters. It sits between fish like Eusthenopteron and true fishapods.
facts: CT scans revealed tiny bones at the tip of its fin that look like the beginnings of fingers.

nodes.name: Tiktaalik
nodes.summary: The famous 'fishapod': a fish with scales and gills, but also a neck, lungs and sturdy fins with wrist joints that could prop it up in the shallows.
facts: Scientists found it in 2004 on Ellesmere Island in the Canadian Arctic, after predicting which age of rocks to search.
Its name comes from the Inuktitut word for a large freshwater fish.
Fossil footprints in Poland are even older, so true four-legged animals may have already existed alongside it.

nodes.name: Acanthostega
nodes.summary: One of the earliest tetrapods: it had legs with fingers but still breathed with gills and lived mostly in water. Legs evolved before walking on land!
facts: Its front feet had eight fingers each.
Its best fossils were found in East Greenland by Jennifer Clack's team in 1987.

nodes.name: Ichthyostega
nodes.summary: A sturdy early tetrapod with a fishy tail and strong shoulders that may have hauled itself across mudflats a bit like a seal.
facts: Its back feet had seven toes.
It was first described in 1932, from fossils found in Greenland.

nodes.name: Temnospondyls
nodes.summary: A hugely successful group of early amphibians, from small insect-eaters to crocodile-sized river predators. Frogs and salamanders probably evolved from among them.
facts: They survived for more than 200 million years, outlasting the start of the dinosaur age.

nodes.name: Eryops
nodes.summary: A heavy, 2-metre amphibian with a broad, toothy skull that lurked in early Permian swamps of what is now Texas.
facts: Its name means 'drawn-out face'.
It is one of the best-known early tetrapods, with many complete skeletons.

nodes.name: Koolasuchus
nodes.summary: One of the very last temnospondyls, a crocodile-sized amphibian living in icy polar rivers of Cretaceous Australia — too cold for crocodiles.
facts: It lived alongside dinosaurs, more than 200 million years after its group first appeared.
It is named after Lesley Kool, who helped dig up fossils in Victoria.

nodes.name: Diplocaulus
nodes.summary: A metre-long, newt-like amphibian with a bizarre boomerang-shaped head. It belonged to the lepospondyls, a different group from temnospondyls.
facts: Its wide head may have worked like a hydrofoil, helping it glide through water.
Babies had small heads; the 'horns' grew wider as they aged.

nodes.name: Modern amphibians
nodes.summary: Frogs, salamanders and caecilians. Most start life in water and change shape as they grow, and all have thin skin through which they can breathe.
facts: There are over 8,000 species of amphibians.
About 40% of amphibian species are threatened with extinction, partly by a deadly chytrid fungus.

nodes.name: Frogs
nodes.summary: Tail-less, long-legged jumpers that start life as tadpoles. Over 7,000 species live everywhere from rainforests to deserts.
facts: Frogs push their eyeballs down into their mouths to help swallow food.
Wood frogs freeze solid in winter, heart stopped, and thaw back to life in spring.
A 250-million-year-old fossil, Triadobatrachus, shows an early proto-frog that still had a short tail.

nodes.name: Toads
nodes.summary: Frogs with dry, warty skin and short legs that walk as much as hop. Big glands behind their eyes ooze poison to deter predators.
facts: About 100 cane toads were brought to Australia in 1935 to eat sugar-cane beetles; there are now over 200 million.
You can't catch warts from touching a toad.

nodes.name: Poison dart frogs
nodes.summary: Tiny, brilliantly coloured rainforest frogs whose bright colours warn: don't eat me! Some have skin toxins among the most powerful in nature.
facts: One golden poison frog carries enough toxin to kill about ten people.
They get their poison from the ants and mites they eat, so frogs raised in captivity are harmless.
Emberá hunters in Colombia tipped blowgun darts with their poison.

nodes.name: Salamanders & newts
nodes.summary: Lizard-shaped amphibians with moist skin and long tails. They are champions of regeneration, regrowing lost legs, tails and even parts of their hearts and eyes.
facts: The biggest family of salamanders has no lungs at all; they breathe through their skin and mouths.
People once believed salamanders could live in fire — probably because they crawled out of burning logs.

nodes.name: Axolotl
nodes.summary: A smiling Mexican salamander that never grows up: it keeps its feathery gills and lives in water its whole life. It can regrow limbs, spinal cord and even parts of its brain.
facts: Its genome is about ten times bigger than a human's.
Common in labs and aquariums, it is critically endangered in the wild, surviving only in canals of Lake Xochimilco in Mexico City.
Its name comes from Xolotl, an Aztec god.

nodes.name: Chinese giant salamander
nodes.summary: Among the largest amphibians on Earth, up to about 1.8 metres long, living in rocky mountain streams in China. Its family dates back to the Jurassic.
facts: In Chinese it's called 'baby fish' because its calls sound like a crying baby.
It is critically endangered, largely because it is farmed and hunted for food.

nodes.name: Caecilians
nodes.summary: Legless, burrowing amphibians that look like giant earthworms. Most live hidden in tropical soils, so few people have ever seen one.
facts: In some species, babies feed by peeling off and eating their mother's outer layer of skin.
Some caecilians have glands at the base of their teeth that may produce venom.
